Literature review: Across 14 randomized trials, spaced repetition improved long-term retention by a median of 18% compared with massed practice [1]. The effect was strongest for vocabulary and factual recall and weaker for procedural skills such as solving algebra problems [2]. Two studies found that expanding intervals outperformed fixed intervals, while three found no significant difference [3]. Retrieval practice combined with feedback produced larger gains than retrieval alone, especially for learners with low prior knowledge [4]. Most trials were short, lasting under twelve weeks, so evidence for retention beyond one year remains limited [5]. Sample sizes ranged from 40 to 1,200 participants, and only four trials were pre-registered, which raises the risk of publication bias [6]. Effects in workplace training were smaller than in university settings, possibly because sessions were less frequent [7]. Overall, the evidence supports spaced retrieval as a low-cost intervention, but longer follow-up studies are needed before strong claims about permanent retention can be made [8].
